newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss fund helps E. Europe Holocaust victims first.
newsitem.headline: Swiss fund helps E. Europe Holocaust victims first.

text.p: Switzerland's Holocaust memorial fund will make a first payment of 17 million Swiss francs ($11.6 million) to help needy victims, primarily in eastern Europe, of the Nazis' murderous wartime campaign, officials said on Monday.

The panel's seven-member executive board made the decision at its inaugural meeting in Berne, voting to pay out 10 percent of its original capital to provide quick help for people in the most desperate straits.

"We can be satisfied because we have sent a signal that we are serious about helping, that things are moving forward, and that we can provide initial assistance to these primarily elderly people," panel chairman Rolf Bloch told Swiss radio.

Bloch told Reuters 15 million francs was earmarked for Jewish recipients and two million for other Holocaust victims, including gypsies and homosexuals. The first recipients could have assistance in hand by September or October, he said.

Panel members cited the special plight of Holocaust survivors in eastern Europe, known as "double victims" for their inability to get compensation during the Cold War for their suffering during Hitler's systematic murder of six million Jews and many others deemed unworthy to live.

The Swiss memorial fund administers around 170 million Swiss francs in donations from commercial banks and other private businesses eager to burnish Switzerland's humanitarian image amid charges the country cynically profited from World War Two.

The Swiss National Bank, which admits it bought Nazi gold it should have known was looted, plans to add another 100 million francs if parliament approves and the plan is not shot down by voters in a referendum that opponents could force.

With the clock inexorably ticking for Holocaust survivors, now averaging 80 years old, there is no time to lose in handing out millions of dollars in humanitarian aid via organisations that deal with Nazis' victims, panel members said.
"This is a probably a big sum. if you think of 17 million, for many in the east that could be a great help for many thousands of people," Bloch told the radio.
"These funds should primarily help the neediest among the needy," a panel statement said, estimating there were around 60,000 "double victims" in eastern Europe who qualify for help.

At a news conference before the meeting, Bloch said he and his colleagues -- three representatives of Jewish groups and three Swiss -- wanted to press ahead even though the fund's secretariat had not yet been formed.
World Jewish Congress (WJC) secretary general Israel Singer, sitting in for WJC President Edgar Bronfman, hailed the panel's no-nonsense approach.

"The efforts that we make here today will augur well for the beginning of a new environment, we hope, between the Jewish people and Switzerland and between the world and Switzerland," he told reporters.
"This will create good public relations because the only good public relations in the world is good public conduct. That is what we are doing here today," he said.

Singer was referring to months of wrangling between Swiss banks and Jewish groups over accusations that banks are hoarding billions of dollars in dormant wealth of Holocaust victims, a charge the financial institutions deny.

The fund is separate from the Swiss government's plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian fund that would use sales of official gold reserves to help victims of poverty, disasters and human rights abuses.
